newsitem.title: USA: Calif. budget fails to provide funds for disasters.
newsitem.headline: Calif. budget fails to provide funds for disasters.

text.p: California Gov. Pete Wilson's $66.6 billion 1997-1998 budget plan is balanced with a modest reserve but does not provide funding for current or future emergencies, the Legislative Analyst said Wednesday.
The Republican governor's proposed general fund budget is balanced with a reserve of $553 million.

The Legislative Analyst's Office, which provides fiscal and policy advice to the California legislature, said the modest reserve was an improvement but was relatively small compared to the size of the budget. "Building a larger reserve should remain a key budgetary priority," the analyst said.

"The governor's proposed reserve of $553 million could be eaten up very quickly," Legislative Analyst Elizabeth Hill told reporters at a briefing. Given today's favorable economic conditions, Hill added, the state should build up the budget reserve in case of emergencies.
Wilson released his proposed 1997-1998 state budget on January 9. It called for funding increases for education and prisons and significant funding reductions for welfare.
The plan also included a 10 percent bank and corporation tax cut phased in during 1998 and 1999. The budget-year cost of the proposal was estimated at $88 million, Hill said.
The annual cost of the proposed tax cut would rise to $647 million in 2000-2001 when the proposal is fully phased in, the Legislative Analyst said.
Wilson's budget forecasts were generally consistent with recent projections made by other economists, although Wilson's personal income forecast was slightly above the consensus.

Hill said the budget's revenue forecast was lower than the Legislative Analyst's forecast by $266 million in 1996-1997 and $399 million in 1997-1998, or $665 million combined. The difference reflected the budget's more conservative sales tax revenue estimates, the Legislative Analyst said.
